title: OpenAI and Anthropic Are Throwing Millions at YC Startups. Indian Founders Are Cashing In — and Reselling the Credits.
excerpt: The AI giants' credit war could cost $800 million a year. For Indian entrepreneurs in Y Combinator, it is a windfall — and for some, a side business.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI and Anthropic are offering up to $2 million in credits to Y Combinator startups.
  • Indian founders are reselling AI credits, creating a grey market for surplus allocations.
  • The credit war could cost AI giants $800 million annually in subsidies.
  • New Indian AI startups are built on existing AI models, speeding up development.
  • Founders prefer Anthropic's no-equity credits to avoid further ownership dilution.

The most expensive customer acquisition campaign in the history of enterprise software is playing out inside Y Combinator's offices, and Indian founders are among its biggest beneficiaries. OpenAI has offered each startup in recent YC batches up to $2 million in API credits — structured as $500,000 free and an additional $1.5 million available in exchange for a small equity stake. Anthropic, unwilling to cede the next generation of builders to its rival, has countered with $500,000 in credits per startup, no equity strings attached. Together, across Y Combinator's four annual cohorts of roughly 200 companies each, the two AI giants could be giving away as much as $800 million a year in compute subsidies. https://x.com/OpenAI/status/2075686461693898868 The scale of the spending reflects a calculation that both companies have made explicitly: whichever platform today's seed-stage founders build on will be the platform their companies still run on at scale. Lock-in at the API layer is the new lock-in, and credits are the weapon of choice. ## The Indian Angle: Windfall and Side Hustle > **"One Indian-American founder, who asked not to be identified because reselling credits may violate terms of service, described the arithmetic bluntly: "I got $1 million in combined credits."** Indian founders have been disproportionately represented in recent YC cohorts, and the credit war has created dynamics that go well beyond legitimate startup use. At YC's Startup School event in Bengaluru earlier this year, attendees received $25,000 in OpenAI credits as part of the programme. Within weeks, some of those credits were being resold on informal channels at 20% to 40% discounts — a grey market that neither OpenAI nor YC has publicly addressed. The resale phenomenon is not limited to Startup School credits. Founders who have received the full $500,000 allocation from both OpenAI and Anthropic — a combined $1 million in API access — sometimes find themselves with more compute than their early-stage product can consume. A founder building a vertical SaaS tool for, say, logistics routing does not need half a million dollars of GPT-4 inference in its first year. The surplus becomes tradeable. One Indian-American founder, who asked not to be identified because reselling credits may violate terms of service, described the arithmetic bluntly: "I got $1 million in combined credits. My actual burn on AI inference is maybe $8,000 a month. I've sold $200,000 worth to three other startups in my network at a 30% discount, and I still have more than I can use before they expire." ## Why This Matters Beyond Silicon Valley The credit war is accelerating a structural shift in how Indian AI startups are being built. In Bengaluru and Hyderabad, a new cohort of founders is building companies whose entire product thesis depends on access to frontier AI models. Unlike the previous generation of Indian SaaS companies — Freshworks, Zoho, Chargebee — which built their own software stacks from scratch, these startups are essentially thin application layers on top of OpenAI or Anthropic's foundation models.
Reselling AI Credits: A New Market
›$1 million in credits received by some founders.
›Resold credits at 20%-40% discounts.
›One founder sold $200,000 worth of credits.
›Actual monthly burn on AI inference: $8,000.
That dependency creates opportunity and risk in equal measure. The opportunity is speed: a team of three engineers in Bengaluru can now build and ship an AI-powered product in weeks that would have taken a 30-person team a year to develop in 2022. The risk is structural. If OpenAI raises its API prices — and the company has signalled that current pricing is not sustainable long-term — every startup built on its platform faces an instant margin compression that no amount of engineering can offset. Anthropic's no-equity offer has particular appeal to Indian founders who are already giving up significant ownership to YC itself (the standard deal is 7% for $500,000) and may be reluctant to dilute further for API credits they view as a commodity. Several founders interviewed for this article said they chose to build on Claude specifically because Anthropic's credits came without equity conditions. ## The Bigger Picture: Platform Wars, Indian-Style The credit war echoes an older pattern familiar to Indian tech. In the early 2010s, Amazon and Flipkart burned billions in discounts to win Indian e-commerce customers. The AI platform equivalent is playing out at the developer level rather than the consumer level, but the logic is identical: subsidise adoption now, extract value later.
Shifting Dynamics in Indian AI Startups
›New startups depend on AI models for product development.
›Speed of development drastically increased.
›Risk of margin compression if API prices rise.
›Founders prefer no-equity offers to avoid dilution.
For Indian AI startups and the diaspora investors backing them, the strategic question is not which platform offers more free credits today. It is which platform will still be competitively priced, technically superior, and reliably available five years from now — when the credits have expired and the real bills start arriving. Y Combinator's next batch opens for applications in September. Indian founders are expected to make up roughly a quarter of applicants.
